Cuba. The largest Caribbean island occupied a strategic position in American foreign policy from the nineteenth century onward, first as a Spanish colony vulnerable to American expansion, then as a newly independent nation caught up in Cold War conflict, becoming a flashpoint of superpower competition.

From 1492 until 1898, Cuba was a Spanish colonial possession that supplied sugar wealth to Madrid and hosted slavery on a massive scale. American interests in Cuban independence grew throughout the nineteenth century, driven by geographic proximity and investment in sugar plantations. When the Spanish-American War ended in 1898, American occupation followed independence, subordinating the island to Washington's oversight rather than truly freeing it.

The island's fortunes shifted dramatically when Fidel Castro's revolution in 1959 severed Cuba from American dominance and aligned the island with the Soviet Union during the Cold War. The following year, the CIA sponsored the Bay of Pigs invasion, a failed attempt to overthrow Castro that spectacularly deepened Cuban-American hostility. Then came the Cuban Missile Crisis in 1962, when the superpowers came to the brink of nuclear war over Soviet missiles deployed on the island.

The American embargo beginning in 1962 economically isolated Cuba, making the island a symbol of anti-imperialism in the global south. Though Castro's regime pursued land reform and educational expansion, it also isolated Cuba internationally. The embargo, maintained for over six decades despite diplomatic opening under Barack Obama, remains one of the world's longest-standing trade sanctions on a single nation. Cuba's alliance with the Soviet Union made it a crucial strategic asset during the Cold War, hosting Soviet troops and missiles aimed at American cities.
